ld.howto_name: How to install Gantry on macOS
ld.howto_desc: Install Gantry with Homebrew and connect it to Docker or Apple container.
ld.howto_supply: A Mac with macOS 26 or later

howto_steps.name: Install with Homebrew
howto_steps.text: Run: brew install --cask getgantry/tap/gantry. Or download the latest release from GitHub and drag Gantry.app into Applications.

howto_steps.name: Clear the quarantine flag
howto_steps.text: The app is not notarized. Run: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Gantry.app, or right-click Gantry.app and choose Open.

howto_steps.name: Add a host
howto_steps.text: Open Gantry. It finds your local Docker daemon. To use Apple container, add an Apple Container host; Gantry offers to set up the container CLI if it is missing.

items.q: What is the best GUI for Apple container?
items.a: Gantry is a free, open-source native macOS GUI made for Apple's container tool (apple/container). It covers the container lifecycle, logs, stats and an exec terminal, plus the parts of the CLI that other GUIs do not reach: Kubernetes clusters (container cluster), container machines, the image builder, registry logins, kernels, service logs and system properties. It supports CLI 1.0 to 1.7.1 and turns each feature on only when your CLI supports it. See the apple/container guide.

items.q: What is Apple container (apple/container)?
items.a: apple/container is Apple's open-source tool for running Linux containers on a Mac. Each container runs in its own lightweight virtual machine, built on Apple's Virtualization framework. It needs a Mac with Apple silicon and ships as a command-line tool named container, with no desktop app. Gantry adds that desktop app.

items.q: Does Gantry support container cluster and Kubernetes?
items.a: Yes. On an apple/container host, Gantry creates and deletes Kubernetes clusters with container cluster (CLI 1.6.1 and 1.7; CLI 1.5.0 to 1.6.0 use container k8s). You choose the name, the workers, the CPUs and memory of the control plane and of the workers (1.7), the node image, the CNI and whether nodes use your local images (1.7). Gantry shows the nodes, writes the kubeconfig and opens the cluster in its Kubernetes browser. See Kubernetes on apple/container.

items.q: Can I use docker compose with Apple container?
items.a: Yes. apple/container has no compose command, so Gantry does the orchestration over the container CLI: it builds build: services, creates the project network and named volumes, and starts each service in depends_on order with the standard Compose labels. Service names resolve through network DNS aliases. Open a docker-compose.yml from Finder, the File menu or by dropping it on the window.

items.q: How do I open a container machine in VS Code?
items.a: Start the machine in Gantry and click Open in VS Code. Gantry opens the machine in VS Code over Remote-SSH, as in Apple's container-machine-vscode example. The machine image must run sshd, and VS Code with the Remote-SSH extension must be installed.

items.q: Which apple/container versions does Gantry support?
items.a: Gantry needs container CLI 1.0 or later and recommends 1.7.1. It reads the installed version and shows only the features that version supports, for example worker sizes and the shared image store (1.7), commit (1.6) and Trim Disk (1.4). If the CLI is missing or old, Gantry offers a guided setup.

items.q: Can Gantry browse a Kubernetes cluster?
items.a: Yes. The Kubernetes section lists pods, deployments, stateful sets, daemon sets, services, ingresses, config maps, secrets, nodes and events for each kubeconfig context, and has pod logs, a pod shell, port forwards, scale, rollout restart, delete and Apply YAML. It works with any cluster, and the contexts of apple/container clusters come first. The browser uses kubectl, and Gantry can install it with Homebrew. See Run Kubernetes on a Mac.
items.a_native: Yes. The Kubernetes section lists pods, deployments, stateful sets, daemon sets, services, ingresses, config maps, secrets, nodes and events for each kubeconfig context, and has pod logs, a pod shell, port forwards, scale, rollout restart, delete and Apply YAML. Gantry talks to the Kubernetes API itself, so you do not need kubectl. See Run Kubernetes on a Mac.

items.q: What does Explain Failure send to Apple Intelligence?
items.a: Recent logs and the container details, with environment values and secret-like text removed. Small requests run on the on-device model. With the setting for long logs on (macOS 27), long logs go to Private Cloud Compute. The panel shows what was sent. A suggested command opens in Terminal but does not run until you press Return. Without Apple Intelligence, Gantry offers a prompt to copy into another AI assistant.

items.q: Can I paste a docker run command into Gantry?
items.a: Yes. In the New Container sheet, choose Paste Command…. Gantry reads docker run, docker create, podman run and container run, fills the form and lists each flag that it cannot use, with the reason. See Create a container from a docker run command.

items.q: Can Gantry manage the apple/container builder, registries and kernel?
items.a: Yes. The System section of an apple/container host starts, stops and deletes the image builder with CPU, memory and DNS options; lists, adds and removes registry logins (the password goes to the CLI on stdin only); installs the recommended kernel, a kernel file or a tar archive; streams service logs; and edits the system properties in config.toml.

items.q: Is Gantry a Docker Desktop, OrbStack or Podman Desktop alternative?
items.a: For the GUI, yes. Gantry is a free, native macOS app for managing containers, images, volumes, networks, logs and stats. It is a client, not an engine: it uses the Docker daemon you already run (Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima) or Apple's container tool, and adds a multi-host view, SSH hosts and an MCP server. See the comparison.

items.q: Is Gantry free?
items.a: Yes. Gantry is free and open source under the MIT license. There is no subscription, no account, and no limit on the number of hosts or containers.

items.q: What do I need to run Gantry?
items.a: macOS 26 or later on Apple silicon or Intel, plus a Docker daemon (Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima or similar) or Apple's container tool. apple/container itself needs Apple silicon, so on an Intel Mac Gantry manages Docker hosts only.

items.q: Does Gantry work with OrbStack, Colima and Docker Desktop?
items.a: Yes. Gantry talks directly to the Docker Engine API over the Unix socket, so it works with any daemon that exposes it, including OrbStack, Colima and Docker Desktop.

items.q: Can Gantry manage remote Docker hosts?
items.a: Yes. Gantry connects to remote daemons over SSH, the same way as docker -H ssh://, with ProxyJump bastions, multi-key auth and auto-reconnect. Nothing needs to be installed on the server, and secrets live in the macOS Keychain.

items.q: Does Gantry alert me when a container fails?
items.a: Yes. Gantry posts a native macOS notification when a container crashes, runs out of memory, or fails its health check on any host: local, SSH or apple/container. Click it to go to the container. Stops and restarts you start from Gantry stay quiet, and you can turn it off in Settings.

items.q: Can Gantry pull from private registries?
items.a: Yes. On Docker hosts, Gantry reads credentials from your ~/.docker/config.json (the same docker login you already ran), including inline auth, credential helpers and the macOS Keychain. On apple/container hosts, it manages container registry logins.

items.q: Can Gantry expose a local container to the internet?
items.a: Yes. One click on a published port shares it over a Cloudflare Tunnel. Gantry installs cloudflared if needed, then starts a quick tunnel (no Cloudflare account, a temporary trycloudflare.com URL) or a named tunnel on your own hostname. The public URL shows under the port with open, copy and stop controls.

items.q: Is Gantry an Electron app?
items.a: No. Gantry is a native app built with SwiftUI and Swift 6. The UI is available in 28 languages: English, Simplified Chinese and 26 European languages, for example Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin script. It follows the macOS system language.

items.q: How do I install Gantry?
items.a: Run brew install --cask getgantry/tap/gantry, or download the latest release from GitHub and drag Gantry.app into Applications.

items.q: Can AI agents control Gantry?
items.a: Yes. Gantry bundles an MCP server and macOS App Intents, so Claude, Shortcuts, Siri and scripts get the same reach as the GUI on every host, including SSH hosts: containers, images, volumes, networks, Compose, apple/container machines, Kubernetes clusters, apple_* system tools (services, builder, registries, properties, logs, kernel) and port sharing. On macOS 26 and later, Explain Failure… also asks Apple Intelligence why a container failed. Add the MCP server with claude mcp add gantry -- /Applications/Gantry.app/Contents/Resources/gantry-mcp.

faq.p: Everything you might want to know before you install Gantry.

items.p: Create, start, stop, kill and prune; live logs, stats, an exec terminal, top and tar export, in the same UI as your Docker hosts.

Create a Kubernetes cluster with container cluster: size the control plane and the workers separately, pick the CNI, and see the nodes, the Kubernetes version and the kubeconfig context. Cluster nodes are locked against accidental stop and delete. Read more
On CLI 1.7, turn on Use local images (--shared-image-store) and pods run the images you build or pull, with no registry. On CLI 1.5 and 1.6, right-click an image and choose Load into Cluster.

items.h: Clear hints when the install is broken
items.p: If the cluster services do not answer, Gantry tells you why. A Homebrew build without the cluster services gets a link to the signed installer; anything else gets a Restart Services button.
Create, start and stop container machine Linux environments, set CPUs and memory, open a shell, or open the machine in VS Code over Remote-SSH.
Boot a machine with nested virtualization (M3 or newer) or your own kernel. Boot containers from a custom kernel with extra boot arguments.

apple/container has no compose. Gantry runs your docker-compose.yml: it builds, creates the network and volumes, and starts services in depends_on order. Service names resolve through network DNS aliases.
Container aliases, subtree aliases such as .gateway, and short names when a default DNS domain is set. Every container gets a routable IP and a name.domain hostname.
See the builder state, image, CPUs, memory and IP. Start it with CPU, memory and DNS options, stop it or delete it. When the builder image is outdated, Gantry offers to recreate it.
List, add and remove container registry logins. The password goes to the CLI on stdin only, and Gantry keeps no copy.
Install the recommended kernel, a kernel file or a tar archive, with live progress. Gantry warns you when no default kernel is installed.
Start, stop and restart the container services, compare client and server versions, and stream service logs filtered by level, service and text.

Edit the container system properties in config.toml. Gantry marks the changes that need a restart and restarts the services for you. On CLI 1.7, it also edits the [container.dns] defaults: name servers, search domains and options.
Commit a container to an image (container commit) and reclaim disk space with Trim Disk (container clean), also in the Reclaim Space panel.
Browse a container's files, download them or drag them out to Finder (container copy), and drop files or whole folders in.
Pick an image, share a folder, map ports and choose a domain, then run. Right-click a compose file in Finder and open it with Gantry.
The container CLI rejects label values with =. Gantry encodes them on create and decodes them on read, so a value such as a=b stays intact.
apple/container hosts sit next to your local Docker and SSH hosts on one dashboard, with the same sparklines, health and failure notifications.
The bundled MCP server gives agents the same reach: containers, machines, clusters, and apple_* system tools for services, builder, registries, properties, logs and kernels.

trust.title: Works with everything you already run

features.h2: Everything Docker and apple/container, the Mac way
features.p: A complete, focused command center for your containers — live by default, fast to the point of feeling local even when it isn't.

fleet.p: Local daemon, SSH fleet and apple/container on one screen — live CPU/memory sparklines, container-state breakdowns, and health issues that jump straight to the culprit.

logs.p: Real-time follow, regex or literal ⌘F search, a level filter (Error→Trace), ANSI color, a 50k-line buffer — and merged stack logs for a whole Compose project.

notify.n2_text: api on dedic failed its health check.
notify.p: A native notification when a container crashes, runs out of memory or goes unhealthy on any host. Click it to jump straight to the container — stops you trigger yourself stay quiet.

stats.p: CPU, memory, network & disk I/O charted live at 1s sampling.

exec.p: Full terminal emulation into any running container, local or remote — with color themes (System, Solarized, Dracula, Nord).

ssh.p: Tunnels exactly like docker -H ssh:// via dial-stdio — ProxyJump bastions, multi-key auth, auto-reconnect. Nothing to install on the server, secrets in the Keychain. One-click import from ~/.ssh/config and docker context ls.

files.p: Browse a container's filesystem, move files in and out, and drop whole folders straight from Finder — on Docker and apple/container hosts alike.

ports.p: One click opens a published port. SSH ports tunnel to localhost automatically — and if it's taken, Gantry picks a free one you can edit.

tunnel.p: One click exposes a published port over a Cloudflare Tunnel. Gantry installs cloudflared for you, then gives a quick tunnel (no account, a *.trycloudflare.com URL) or a named tunnel on your own domain — perfect for a dev preview, a webhook, or letting an AI agent reach a container on your Mac.

compose.p: Containers group by their Compose project. Bring a compose file up on any host — local Docker, SSH or apple/container — with an inline YAML editor; the runner adapts per engine.

registries.p: Pulls read the docker login you already did — Gantry resolves credentials from ~/.docker/config.json, helpers and the Keychain, on create, Quick Run and Compose alike.

images.p: Drop a Dockerfile on the window to build with a live log, or pull by reference with per-layer progress. Tag, prune and read layer history. A badge marks images built for a different CPU architecture than the host.

cleanup.p: One panel shows what is taking space — dangling images, stopped containers, unused volumes, build cache — with sizes, and prunes each or all. On apple/container it also runs Trim Disk.

touchid.p: Opt in and Gantry asks for Touch ID — or your login password — before removing a container or deleting a host. Secrets already live in the Keychain.

themes.p: Dress the embedded shell in System, Solarized Dark, Dracula or Nord — a full foreground, background and 16-color ANSI palette, applied live.

agents.h2: Built to be driven by AI
agents.p: A bundled MCP server and App Intents expose every host — including SSH ones — to Claude, Shortcuts, Siri and scripts, with the same reach as the GUI: create and manage containers, build and pull images, volumes and networks, Compose up, apple/container machines and Kubernetes clusters, the apple_* system tools for services, builder, registries and kernels, even exposing a port over a Cloudflare Tunnel.
agents.term_title: Terminal — wire up the MCP server
agents.prompt_p: Hit ⌥⌘P on any container and Gantry puts a paste-ready debugging prompt on your clipboard — the host and how to reach it, the MCP host_id and tools, the container's full state, and a task matched to the symptom.
agents.s3_text: Leaves room for your own question.

shots.p: Three-column split view, Swift Charts, Liquid Glass only on floating controls. Real screenshots, no mockups.

built.h2: No web wrappers. No daemons of our own.
built.p: Just a fast, native Mac app talking straight to the Docker Engine API and to Apple's container CLI.
built.swiftui_p: Not Electron. Launches instantly, sips memory, feels like the OS.
built.swift6_p: Modern, concurrency-safe codebase on the latest toolchain.
built.api_p: Docker over the Unix socket, no Docker CLI needed. apple/container through its own container CLI.
built.updates_p: EdDSA-signed Sparkle appcast keeps you current, out of your way.

install.s1_text: Run the Homebrew cask, or grab the .zip from Releases and drag Gantry.app to Applications.
install.s2_text: Not notarized yet — right-click & Open, or clear quarantine with xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Gantry.app
install.s3_text: Local Docker shows up by itself. For Apple container, add an Apple Container host; Gantry offers to set up the container CLI. Agents: claude mcp add gantry.

new.h2: Kubernetes, Apple Intelligence and the rest of macOS
new.p: Gantry 0.27.0 adds a Kubernetes browser, explains failed containers with Apple Intelligence, and works with Spotlight, Siri, widgets and Control Center. It supports apple/container 1.7.1 and has a new design that follows Apple's Human Interface Guidelines.

kube.p: Browse pods, deployments, stateful sets, daemon sets, services, ingresses, config maps, secrets, nodes and events of any kubeconfig context. Follow pod logs, open a shell, forward a port, scale, restart a rollout and apply YAML. Secret values stay masked until you reveal them. The browser uses kubectl; if it is missing, Gantry installs it with Homebrew.
kube.p_native: Browse pods, deployments, stateful sets, daemon sets, services, ingresses, config maps, secrets, nodes and events of any kubeconfig context. Follow pod logs, open a shell, forward a port, scale, restart a rollout and apply YAML. Gantry talks to the Kubernetes API itself, so a cluster made with container cluster create is ready to browse with nothing else installed: no kubectl.

explain.p: Choose Explain Failure… on a crashed container or a failed operation. Gantry sends recent logs and details, with environment values and secret-like text removed, to the on-device model, and shows the likely cause, the evidence and next steps. Long logs can go to Private Cloud Compute (macOS 27). The panel shows exactly what was sent.

macos.p: Notifications with Restart, View Logs and Copy as Prompt. Spotlight finds containers, Compose projects and hosts. Siri and Shortcuts actions, a fleet health widget, Control Center controls for the apple/container services or a favorite container, and gantry:// links for scripts.

palette.p: Press ⌘K and type. One search covers containers, Compose projects, images, volumes, networks, machines, clusters and hosts, with actions such as Start, Show Logs and Open Shell.

bulk.p: Select several containers, images, volumes or networks and start, stop, restart or remove them in one step, with progress and a report for each item.

paste.p: Paste a docker run, podman run or container run command and Gantry fills the New Container form, with a list of the flags it cannot use. Copy any container back as a command, or save it as a recipe. How it works

storage.p: Move all apple/container data to an external disk, keep volumes on a disk of your choice, and get a clear warning when that disk is not connected. Read the guide

body.h1: Apple container on Mac: the complete guide and GUI
body.lead: apple/container runs Linux containers on your Mac, each in its own lightweight virtual machine. It ships as a command-line tool. Gantry is a native macOS GUI for it. This guide explains the tool, how to set it up, and which Gantry feature covers each container command.
body.tldr: In short. Gantry is a free, open-source (MIT) macOS app that manages Apple's container tool and Docker from one window. It supports container CLI 1.0 to 1.7.1 (recommended) and shows only the features your CLI version supports. Install it with brew install --cask getgantry/tap/gantry.

what-is.p1: apple/container is an open-source tool from Apple, written in Swift, that creates and runs Linux containers on a Mac. Docker Desktop runs all containers in one shared Linux VM; apple/container runs each container in its own lightweight virtual machine, built on Apple's Virtualization framework. It uses standard OCI images, so it pulls from and pushes to the same registries as Docker.
what-is.li3: Interface: the container CLI only. There is no desktop app and no compose command.
what-is.li4: Networking: each container gets its own IP address on your Mac, and local DNS domains give containers names such as web.test.

why-gui.h: Why use a GUI for apple/container?
why-gui.p1: The CLI is complete, but daily work means many commands: container list, logs, stats, exec, then system, builder, registry, machine and cluster for the rest. Gantry puts them in one window with live updates, so you see the state instead of polling for it. It also adds what the CLI does not have: Compose files, failure notifications, a fleet view with your Docker hosts, and an MCP server for AI agents.

setup.li1: Install Gantry: brew install --cask getgantry/tap/gantry, then clear the quarantine flag (see Install).
setup.li2: Install the container CLI from the signed .pkg on the apple/container releases page. If it is missing or older than 1.0, Gantry shows a setup sheet with the steps.
setup.li3: In Gantry, choose Add Host… and add an Apple Container host. Connecting starts the container services if they are stopped.
setup.li4: If no default kernel is installed, the host overview shows a banner. Click it to install the recommended kernel.

command-map.h: Each container command and its Gantry feature
command-map.p1: This table maps the container CLI to Gantry. The last column shows the CLI version that Gantry needs for the feature. Any means any supported CLI, 1.0 or later. Gantry reads your installed version and hides the features that it does not support.

kubernetes.p1: Create Kubernetes clusters with container cluster, size the workers, let pods use your local images, choose the CNI and see each node. Then browse the cluster in the Gantry Kubernetes browser. See Kubernetes on apple/container and the step-by-step guide Run Kubernetes on a Mac.

machines.p1: Machines are long-lived Linux environments from container machine. Gantry creates, starts, stops and deletes them, sets the default machine, edits CPUs and memory, and opens a shell. On CLI 1.1 or later, a machine can boot with nested virtualization (Apple silicon M3 or newer) and a custom kernel. Open in VS Code connects to a running machine over Remote-SSH; the machine image must run sshd.

compose.p1: Open a docker-compose.yml from Finder (Open With ▸ Gantry or Quick Actions ▸ Compose Up in apple/container), from File ▸ Open Compose File…, or by dropping it on the window. Gantry builds build: services, creates the project network and named volumes, and starts each service in depends_on order with the standard com.docker.compose.* labels. With a default DNS domain set, services reach each other by service name through network aliases.

dns.h: Network DNS aliases and local domains
dns.p1: Gantry passes network aliases to container as --network <name>,alias=…. Without a default DNS domain, only fully qualified names pass, and a subtree alias (a leading dot, such as .gateway) passes only as its exact alias. With a default domain, short names work too. Gantry creates and deletes local DNS domains, sets the default domain, and gives new containers a name.domain hostname. See Local DNS names.

system.h: System: services, builder, registries, kernel, logs, properties
system.p1: Each apple/container host has a System section. It works while the host is disconnected, so you can start stopped services from there.
system.li1: Status and version: client and server versions, with a warning when they differ; start, stop and restart the services; host facts and paths.
system.li2: Image Builder: state, image, CPUs, memory and IP; start with CPU, memory and DNS options; stop; delete. A card tells you when the builder image is outdated and recreates it.
system.li3: Registry Logins: list, log in and log out. The password goes to the CLI on stdin (--password-stdin) only, and Gantry keeps no copy.
system.li4: Kernel: install the recommended kernel, a kernel file or a tar archive, with streamed progress.
system.li5: Service Logs: live or one-shot, over 5 minutes to 1 day, filtered by level, service and text.
system.li6: System Properties: edits go to ~/.config/container/config.toml, with a pending-restart flag and a Restart Services button. On CLI 1.7, the [container.dns] name servers, search domains and options have a list editor.

disk.p1: Commit to Image uses container commit (CLI 1.6). Trim Disk uses container clean (CLI 1.4) and also shows as a row in Reclaim Space. The Files tab downloads files and lets you drag them out to Finder with container copy (the container must be started), and uploads files and folders.

labels.p1: container create rejects a label value that contains =, also on CLI 1.6.1. Gantry encodes such values when it creates the container and decodes them when it reads it back, so the labels you set are the labels you see.

agents.p1: The bundled gantry-mcp server gives AI agents the same reach on apple/container hosts: containers, images, volumes, networks, Compose, machines (list_machines, create_machine and more), clusters (list_clusters, create_cluster, delete_cluster) and apple_* system tools for services, builder, registries (no login tool), properties, logs and kernel install. App Intents add Shortcuts and Siri actions. See AI agents & MCP.

vs-docker.p1: Gantry manages apple/container hosts, the local Docker daemon (Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima) and remote Docker hosts over SSH in one sidebar and one fleet dashboard. You do not have to choose one runtime. For a feature-by-feature view of the tools, see Gantry vs Docker Desktop, OrbStack and Podman Desktop. To move your work over, read Move from Docker Desktop to Apple container.

k8s.title: Kubernetes on Apple container: a GUI for container cluster and a Kubernetes browser
k8s.desc: Run Kubernetes on Apple's container tool with Gantry: create clusters with sized workers and the shared image store, browse pods and logs, open a shell, forward ports and apply YAML.
table: CLI 1.7+. Before 1.7, --cpus and --memory set every node
Control plane (CLI 1.7+), or every node (before 1.7), for example 4G
CLI 1.7+. Nodes run images from your local image store
Default (bundled kindnet), None (NONE, CLI 1.6.0+) or a custom manifest path

faq.q: Does Apple container support Kubernetes?
faq.a: Yes. The container CLI creates Kubernetes clusters whose nodes run as containers: container cluster in CLI 1.6.1 and 1.7, container k8s in CLI 1.5.0 to 1.6.0. Gantry gives this a GUI.

faq.q: Does Gantry support container cluster?
faq.a: Yes. Gantry lists, creates and deletes clusters on apple/container hosts, shows their nodes, writes the kubeconfig and opens the cluster in its Kubernetes browser. On CLI 1.7 it also sizes the workers and turns on the shared image store. It uses cluster or k8s to match your CLI version.

faq.q: How do I use kubectl with an apple/container cluster?
faq.a: When the CLI creates a cluster, it adds a kubeconfig context named after the cluster to ~/.kube/config. Run kubectl --context <name> get nodes. To keep a separate file, use Write Kubeconfig in Gantry; the default path is ~/.kube/<name>.kubeconfig.

faq.q: How do I get a local image into the cluster without a registry?
faq.a: On CLI 1.7, create the cluster with Use local images (--shared-image-store). Pods then run the images you build or pull with container, by name. On CLI 1.5 and 1.6, right-click the image in Images and choose Load into Cluster; Gantry runs container cluster load-image. CLI 1.7 removed load-image.

faq.q: Can I create a multi-node cluster?
faq.a: Yes. Set the number of workers in the create sheet; workers need CLI 1.6.0 or later. On CLI 1.7, you also set the CPUs and memory of the workers apart from the control plane.

faq.q: Can I use my own CNI such as Calico or Cilium?
faq.a: Yes. Choose Custom manifest and select the manifest file, or choose None and apply a CNI yourself after the cluster starts. Nodes stay NotReady until a CNI runs. None needs CLI 1.6.0 or later. The default CNI is the bundled kindnet manifest.

faq.q: Why does Gantry say the cluster services are unavailable?
faq.a: The container services did not answer a cluster command. If your CLI is a Homebrew build without the cluster services, Gantry says so and links to the signed installer on the apple/container releases page. Otherwise it offers Restart Services.

faq.q: Do I need kubectl to use the cluster in Gantry?
faq.a: For now, yes: the Gantry Kubernetes browser runs kubectl. If it is not installed, the browser shows the brew install kubectl command and can run it for you.
faq.a_native: No. Gantry talks to the Kubernetes API itself: it reads the kubeconfig, then lists resources, streams logs, opens a shell, forwards ports and applies YAML without kubectl. A cluster made with container cluster create is ready to browse right away.

body.lead: apple/container can run a Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are containers on your Mac. Gantry is a GUI for it: create a cluster, watch its nodes come up, run your local images in it, and browse its pods, logs and services, without long container cluster command lines.
body.tldr: In short. On an apple/container host, the Gantry Clusters section creates and deletes Kubernetes clusters with container cluster (CLI 1.6.1 and 1.7) or container k8s (CLI 1.5.0 to 1.6.0). On CLI 1.7.1 it sizes the workers apart from the control plane and turns on the shared image store. The Kubernetes section browses the cluster: pods, logs, shell, port forwards, scale and Apply YAML.

requirements.li1: A Mac with Apple silicon, macOS 26, and Gantry (brew install --cask getgantry/tap/gantry).
requirements.li2: The container CLI 1.5.0 or later; 1.7.1 is recommended. Workers and the None CNI need 1.6.0 or later. Worker sizes and the shared image store need 1.7.0 or later. Use the signed installer package: the Homebrew build of 1.7.1 has no cluster services.
requirements.li3: kubectl for the Kubernetes browser and the terminal. Gantry can install it with Homebrew.
requirements.li3_native: Nothing else for the Gantry Kubernetes browser. kubectl only if you also want to use the cluster from the terminal.

create.li1: Select your apple/container host and open Clusters in the sidebar.
create.li2: Start a new cluster and fill in the options below.
create.li3: Create it. The list shows the new cluster with streamed progress. Cancel stops the creation and deletes the nodes that were already made.
create.p1: The same command on the CLI:

nodes.p1: The cluster list shows one row for each cluster. The detail view has an Overview (kubectl context, API server, Kubernetes version, image store, workers and their resources, node network), a Nodes table and Inspect for the raw node data. The toolbar has Browse Resources, and the More menu has Write Kubeconfig, Copy kubectl Context Command and Delete.
nodes.p2: Cluster nodes are containers, but container cluster owns them. Gantry disables start, stop, restart, remove and rename for a node and tells you why, and Start All and Stop All skip nodes. On CLI 1.7 the CLI also hides nodes from container list. Clusters created with CLI 1.6 or earlier do not show in the 1.7 list; remove them with container cluster delete --name <name>.

kubectl.p1: The CLI adds a context named after the cluster to ~/.kube/config when it creates the cluster. Use Copy kubectl Context Command in Gantry, or type it:
kubectl.p2: To keep the cluster in its own file, use Write Kubeconfig. Gantry runs container cluster write-config; the default path is ~/.kube/<name>.kubeconfig.

images.h: Use local images in the cluster
images.p1: On CLI 1.7, turn on Use local images when you create the cluster. It adds --shared-image-store, so the nodes can run any image that you build or pull with container, by name, with no registry. The setting is fixed at creation. After you rebuild a tag, use imagePullPolicy: Always or a new tag. Privileged pods can read every image in your local store, so keep this for local development.
images.p2: On CLI 1.5 and 1.6, right-click the image in Images and choose Load into Cluster. Gantry runs container cluster load-image, which copies the image into the containerd of each node. CLI 1.7 removed this command, so Gantry hides the action there.

cni.p1: The default is the bundled kindnet manifest. Choose Custom manifest to install your own CNI, for example Calico or Cilium, from a file. Choose None to install a CNI yourself later; until then, the nodes stay NotReady.

agents.p1: The Gantry MCP server has list_clusters, create_cluster and delete_cluster, so an agent such as Claude Code can make a temporary cluster for a test and remove it after.

more.p1: For a step-by-step walk-through from the terminal, read Run Kubernetes on a Mac with Apple container. Read the apple/container guide for each container command and its Gantry feature, or see how Gantry compares with Docker Desktop, OrbStack and Podman Desktop.

browser.p1: Click Browse Resources on a running cluster, or open Kubernetes in the sidebar. The section needs no host, and it lists every kubeconfig context; the contexts of apple/container clusters come first. Pick a namespace or all namespaces, then a kind: pods, deployments, stateful sets, daemon sets, services, ingresses, config maps, secrets, nodes or events.
browser.li1: Pods: logs with follow, tail and the previous container; a shell in the pod; port forward to 127.0.0.1.
browser.li2: Workloads: scale deployments and stateful sets; restart a rollout.
browser.li3: Secrets: values are masked in the list and in the YAML until you click Reveal.
browser.li4: Apply YAML: paste a manifest or open a file; errors show in the sheet.
browser.p2: The browser runs kubectl. If Gantry cannot find it, the section shows brew install kubectl with a button that runs it.
browser.p2_native: Gantry talks to the Kubernetes API itself, with the credentials in your kubeconfig. You do not need kubectl or any other tool: a cluster made with container cluster create is ready to browse.

broken.h: When the cluster services do not answer
broken.p1: If a cluster command fails with cluster service unavailable, Gantry checks how the CLI is installed. A Homebrew build without the cluster plugins gets the message that the build lacks the cluster services and a Download Installer… link to the signed package. In other cases, Gantry offers Restart Services….

k8s.shot_alt: Cluster overview in Gantry with the Kubernetes version, the image store and the workers
k8s.shot_caption: Cluster overview. Kubernetes version, image store, workers and their resources.

terminal.title: Run Kubernetes on a Mac with Apple container: a step-by-step guide
terminal.desc: Create a local Kubernetes cluster on your Mac with Apple's container cluster: workers, CPUs and memory, local images without a registry, kubectl, and a GUI to browse pods and logs.
terminal.h1: Run Kubernetes on a Mac with Apple container
terminal.lead: Apple's container tool can create a local Kubernetes cluster in one command. Each node is a lightweight virtual machine on your Mac. This guide goes from an empty Mac to a running deployment, first in the terminal and then in Gantry.
terminal.tldr: In short. Install the signed container 1.7.1 package, run container cluster create --name dev --cpus 2 --memory 2g --workers count=2,cpus=2,memory=2g --shared-image-store, build an image with container build and run it in the cluster by name. Gantry shows the same cluster in a window: nodes, pods, logs, a shell and port forwards.

ul: A Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 26 or later.

The container CLI 1.7.1 from the signed .pkg on the apple/container releases page. The Homebrew build of 1.7.1 does not include the cluster services, so container cluster fails with cluster service unavailable.
About 6 GB of free memory for the example below: three nodes with 2 GB each.
kubectl if you want to use the cluster from the terminal (brew install kubectl).

blocks.after: Start the services once after you install the package:

blocks.p: This command makes a cluster named dev with one control-plane node and two workers. Each node gets 2 CPUs and 2 GB of memory:

ul: --workers count=N,cpus=C,memory=M sizes a group of workers. Repeat it for groups of different sizes. Without --workers, one node is both control plane and worker.
--cpus and --memory size the control plane. The default is a quarter of the CPUs and memory of your Mac, at least 2 CPUs and 2 GB.
--shared-image-store lets the nodes use your local images (see below). You cannot change it later: delete the cluster and create it again.
--cni ./calico.yaml installs your own CNI instead of the bundled kindnet; --cni NONE installs none.

blocks.p: The CLI adds a context named dev to ~/.kube/config. Check the nodes:

sections.h: Run a local image without a registry

blocks.p: With --shared-image-store, the nodes can run any image in your local container image store. Build an image and use it by name:

blocks.note: After you rebuild the same tag, run kubectl rollout restart with imagePullPolicy: Always, or use a new tag. With IfNotPresent, a node keeps the copy it already has. Anything with root on a node can read every image in your local store, including private images, so use the shared store for local development only.

blocks.p: On CLI 1.5 and 1.6 there is no shared store. Use container cluster load-image there, or Load into Cluster in Gantry. CLI 1.7 removed load-image.

sections.h: Open the app in a browser

blocks.p: Forward a local port to the deployment, then open http://localhost:8080:

Gantry shows the same cluster without commands. Add your apple/container host, open Clusters, and select dev. The overview shows the Kubernetes version, the image store, the workers and their CPUs and memory. Click Browse Resources to open the Kubernetes section on that context.

ul: Pods, deployments, stateful sets, daemon sets, services, ingresses, config maps, secrets, nodes and events, for one namespace or all of them.
Pod logs with follow and tail, a shell in the pod, and port forwards with a list that you can stop.
Scale, rollout restart, delete, and Apply YAML from a pasted manifest or a file.
Secret values stay masked until you click Reveal.

blocks.p: The Kubernetes browser runs kubectl. If it is missing, Gantry shows brew install kubectl and can run it for you.
Gantry talks to the Kubernetes API itself, so the cluster is ready to browse right after container cluster create. You do not need kubectl or any other tool.

blocks.alt: Gantry Kubernetes browser with the pods of the dev cluster
blocks.caption: Kubernetes browser. The pods of a container cluster with logs and port forwards.

blocks.p: You can also create the cluster in Gantry: Clusters ▸ New Cluster has steppers for the control plane and the workers and a Use local images switch. More on the Kubernetes on apple/container page.
If the control-plane node stops, for example after container system stop, delete the cluster and create it again. Create a throw-away cluster with --rm to remove its nodes when they stop.

ul: cluster service unavailable: the CLI is the Homebrew build, or the services are not running. Install the signed package, or restart the services with container system stop and container system start. Gantry shows the same advice in Clusters.
An old cluster is missing from the list: CLI 1.7 does not list clusters created with 1.6 or earlier. Remove one with container cluster delete --name <name>.
Nodes stay NotReady: you used --cni NONE. Apply a CNI manifest.
You cannot stop a node container: this is on purpose. container stop and delete refuse cluster nodes; use container cluster delete.

sections.h: How this compares with Docker Desktop and OrbStack

blocks.p: Docker Desktop has built-in Kubernetes with kubeadm (one node) or kind (several nodes), and OrbStack has a built-in single-node cluster. container cluster runs kubeadm on kindest/node images, each node in its own VM, with multi-node clusters and the shared image store. See the full comparison.

faq.q: Can I run Kubernetes on a Mac without Docker?
faq.a: Yes. Apple's container CLI creates Kubernetes clusters itself with container cluster create. Each node runs as a lightweight VM, and you do not need Docker, Docker Desktop, kind or minikube.

faq.q: How many nodes can a container cluster have?
faq.a: One control plane and as many workers as your Mac has CPUs and memory for. Set them with --workers; on CLI 1.7 each group of workers can have its own CPUs and memory.

faq.q: How do I use a locally built image in the cluster?
faq.a: Create the cluster with --shared-image-store (CLI 1.7), build the image with container build -t name:tag . and use name:tag in the pod spec. No registry is needed.

faq.q: Which Kubernetes version does container cluster use?
faq.a: CLI 1.7.1 uses the kindest/node:v1.35.5 node image by default. Choose another version with --node-image, for example docker.io/kindest/node:v1.34.11. Gantry shows the version in the cluster overview.

faq.q: Is there a GUI for container cluster?
faq.a: Yes. Gantry creates and deletes clusters, shows the nodes, and browses pods, deployments, services, logs and secrets in its Kubernetes section. It is free and open source.

compare.title: Gantry vs Docker Desktop vs OrbStack vs Podman Desktop on Mac (2026)
compare.desc: A sourced comparison of Gantry, Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Podman Desktop and Apple's container CLI on macOS: license, price, UI, apple/container support, Kubernetes, Compose, external drives and AI.

Docker engine in a Linux VM, plus a GUI
Docker and Linux engine, plus a GUI

Proprietary. Free for personal use, education, non-commercial open source and organizations with fewer than 250 employees and less than $10M annual revenue; otherwise a paid plan (Pro $11, Team $16, Business $24 per user per month)
Proprietary. Free for personal, non-commercial use; Pro for commercial use is $8 per user per month

Yes, with the Apple container extension (through the Socktainer Docker API shim, Apple silicon)

faq.q: Is Gantry a Docker Desktop alternative?
faq.a: For the GUI, yes. Gantry manages containers, images, volumes, networks, logs, stats and Compose. It does not include a Docker engine: on a Mac, use OrbStack, Colima or Docker Desktop for that, or use Apple's container tool, which Gantry also manages. Gantry is MIT licensed and free for commercial use.

faq.q: Is Gantry an OrbStack alternative?
faq.a: Partly. OrbStack is an engine and a GUI; Gantry is a GUI only. You can use Gantry as the GUI on top of the OrbStack Docker engine, or use Gantry with apple/container, which gives you containers, Linux machines and Kubernetes from Apple's own tool.

faq.q: Which is the best GUI for Apple container?
faq.a: Of the tools on this page, Gantry and Podman Desktop (with its Apple container extension) manage apple/container; there are also smaller open-source apps. Gantry covers the whole container CLI: containers, Compose files, Kubernetes clusters, machines, the image builder, registry logins, kernels and system properties, and it follows each new CLI release (1.7.1 as of 2026-11-07).

faq.q: Can I use Gantry and Docker Desktop together?
faq.a: Yes. Gantry connects to the Docker Desktop engine over its socket, so you can use Gantry as the GUI and keep Docker Desktop as the engine.

faq.q: Which of these tools can keep data on an external drive?
faq.a: Docker Desktop has a disk image location setting and OrbStack added a data location in 0.13.0. With apple/container, container system start --app-root puts all data on another disk, and bind mounts work from any disk. See Store containers and volumes on an external drive.

body.h1: Gantry vs Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Podman Desktop and the container CLI
body.lead: Five ways to run and manage containers on a Mac, compared on facts you can check. Gantry is a GUI client. The others include an engine, except the container CLI, which is an engine with no GUI.
body.tldr: In short. Pick Gantry if you want a free, native, open-source GUI for Apple's container tool and for Docker (local and over SSH) in one app. Gantry does not replace a Docker engine; it works with the one you have, or with apple/container.

table.p1: Facts as of 2026-11-07, from each vendor's public pages (see sources). "Unknown" means we did not find the fact in the vendor's documentation. It does not mean that the feature is missing.

choose1.p1: You use Apple's container tool and want a GUI for all of it, including Kubernetes clusters, machines and the image builder. Or you manage several Docker hosts, local and remote over SSH, and want one native window and failure notifications for all of them. Or you want an MCP server and Apple Intelligence to help you find why a container failed. Moving from Docker Desktop? Read Move from Docker Desktop to Apple container.

choose2.p1: You need the Docker engine with the same app on macOS, Windows and Linux, Docker extensions and Docker support, and your company has a Docker subscription or qualifies for free use.

choose3.p1: You want a Docker engine and Linux machines on macOS in one product, and a paid license for commercial use is acceptable.

choose4.p1: You use Podman, want an open-source GUI on several operating systems, or work with Red Hat tools. Its Apple container extension also reaches apple/container containers.

choose5.p1: You script everything in the terminal and do not need a GUI. Gantry uses the same CLI, so you can add the GUI later.

together.p1: Gantry is a client, so it works next to the others. It connects to the Docker engine of Docker Desktop, OrbStack or Colima through the Docker socket, to remote Docker hosts over SSH, and to apple/container through the container CLI, all in one sidebar.

items: Docker Desktop license and prices: Docker Desktop license agreement and Docker pricing.
Docker Desktop features: Kubernetes, settings (disk image location), MCP Toolkit, release notes.
Podman Desktop: source code, Kubernetes, remote connections, Apple container extension, releases.

Yes, for the clusters it connects to

Yes, for the clusters it connects to

table_storage_shipped: Yes: moves the apple/container data root, keeps volumes on any disk, warns when the disk is not connected

docker-desktop-to-apple-container.title: Move from Docker Desktop to Apple container: commands, Compose, volumes and gaps
docker-desktop-to-apple-container.desc: Switch from Docker Desktop to Apple's container tool on a Mac: which docker command maps to which container command, how to bring images, volumes and Compose files over, and what is still missing.
docker-desktop-to-apple-container.h1: Move from Docker Desktop to Apple container
docker-desktop-to-apple-container.lead: Apple's container tool runs the same OCI images as Docker, so most of your work moves over with a few command changes. This guide maps Docker to container, moves images and volumes, and lists the gaps that you should know about before you switch.
docker-desktop-to-apple-container.tldr: In short. Install the signed container package, replace docker with container for run, build, logs, exec and images, copy named volumes with a tar file, and open your docker-compose.yml in Gantry, because the CLI has no compose. You can keep Docker Desktop installed while you try it.

ul: One VM per container. Docker Desktop runs all containers in one Linux VM. apple/container starts a small VM for each container, so each one gets its own IP address on your Mac.
Same images and registries. Images are OCI images; you pull from Docker Hub, GHCR and private registries as before.
No license fee. apple/container is Apache 2.0. Docker Desktop needs a paid plan in organizations with 250 or more employees or $10M or more in revenue.
Apple silicon and macOS 26 only. On Intel Macs, stay with a Docker engine.

sections.h: Docker commands and their container equivalents

blocks.p: Most flags of run are the same: -d, -p, -e, -v, --name, --rm, -it, -w, --entrypoint, --cpus and -m. To convert a long command, paste it in Gantry: see Create a container from a docker run command.

Images from a registry: pull them again with container image pull. Local images that exist only in Docker: save them to an archive and load it. container image load reads OCI archives, and recent Docker versions write an OCI layout with docker save. If the load fails, push the image to a registry and pull it.
Docker keeps volume data inside its VM. Copy each volume to a tar file with a short-lived container, then unpack it into a new apple/container volume:

A named volume in apple/container is a sparse ext4 disk image, 512 GB at most by default. Set another size with --opt size=20g. Bind mounts of folders on your Mac work as in Docker: -v ~/project:/app.

The container CLI has no compose command. Open the docker-compose.yml in Gantry instead (Finder, File ▸ Open Compose File… or drag and drop). Gantry builds the build: services, creates the project network and named volumes, and starts the services in depends_on order. Services reach each other by service name through network DNS aliases.

ul: -p 8080:80 publishes a port on localhost, as in Docker.
Each container also has its own IP address. Create a local DNS domain with sudo container system dns create test and run containers with --dns-domain test: they get names such as web.test.
container network create makes user networks; containers on the same network reach each other.
There is no --network host, none or container: mode.
No Docker Engine API. Tools that talk to /var/run/docker.sock, such as Testcontainers, the Docker SDKs or Dev Containers, do not see apple/container.
No restart policies. --restart is not available; a container does not start again on its own.
No Compose in the CLI. Gantry runs Compose files: see Compose files.
No Docker Desktop extensions.
Whole CPUs only: --cpus 0.5 does not work.
Kubernetes is different: use container cluster, see Run Kubernetes on a Mac.

blocks.p: Gantry manages apple/container and any Docker engine (Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima, or Docker over SSH) in one sidebar. Move one project at a time, and keep Docker for the tools that need its API. When you no longer need it, you can remove Docker Desktop.

faq.q: Can Apple container replace Docker Desktop?
faq.a: For running, building and pulling containers on Apple silicon, yes. It does not have the Docker Engine API, restart policies, extensions or a compose command. Gantry adds Compose files and a GUI.

faq.q: Do Docker images work with Apple container?
faq.a: Yes. apple/container uses standard OCI images and pulls from the same registries. arm64 images run natively; amd64 images run through Rosetta with --arch amd64.

faq.q: Does docker compose work with Apple container?
faq.a: Not from the CLI: there is no container compose. Gantry reads the docker-compose.yml and runs the services on apple/container for you.

faq.q: Can I use Docker Desktop and Apple container at the same time?
faq.a: Yes. They do not share images or volumes, but they can run side by side. Gantry shows both in one window.

faq.q: Is Apple container free for commercial use?
faq.a: Yes. apple/container is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, and Gantry is MIT licensed. Both are free for companies of any size.

containers-on-external-drive.title: Store containers and volumes on an external drive on a Mac
containers-on-external-drive.desc: Keep Apple container images, containers and volumes on an external SSD: find the data root, move it with container system start --app-root, use bind mounts, and unplug the disk safely.
containers-on-external-drive.h1: Store containers and volumes on an external drive
containers-on-external-drive.lead: Images, containers and volumes fill a small internal disk fast. With Apple's container tool you can keep that data on an external SSD: put single folders there with bind mounts, or move the whole data root. This guide shows both, and how to unplug the disk without damage.
containers-on-external-drive.tldr: In short. Format the disk as APFS. For one project, bind-mount a folder: -v /Volumes/Fast/pg:/data. For everything, stop the services, copy ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.container to the disk with cp -Rp, and start the services with container system start --app-root /Volumes/Fast/container each time.

blocks.p: apple/container keeps all its data in one folder, the app root. By default it is ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.container, with folders for containers, image content, snapshots, volumes, kernels and networks. Check the path and the space in use:

ul: Use an SSD on USB-C or Thunderbolt. A spinning disk works, but containers start slower.
Format it as APFS (Mac OS Extended works too). Do not use exFAT, FAT or NTFS: volumes are sparse disk images, and those file systems have no sparse files and no Unix permissions.
Do not use a network disk for the app root.
Give the disk a short name without spaces, for example Fast. The path is then /Volumes/Fast.

sections.h: Option 1: keep project data on the disk with bind mounts

blocks.p: A bind mount shares a folder of your Mac with the container, and the folder can be on any disk. This is the easy way to keep large data, such as a database or model files, off the internal disk:
The disk must be connected before the container starts. Images and the container itself stay on the internal disk.

sections.h: Option 2: move all apple/container data to the disk

blocks.p: This moves images, containers, snapshots and volumes. Stop the services first, so no file changes during the copy:

Use cp -Rp. In our test on macOS 27 (APFS to APFS over USB), it kept the volume images sparse and kept the extended attributes. ditto wrote each sparse image at its full size, which can fill the disk. Keep the old folder until you have checked that your containers, images and volumes are listed.

blocks.warn: The CLI does not remember --app-root. Each container system start without it uses the internal folder again. Use the flag every time, for example in a shell alias, and check paths.appRoot in container system status.

blocks.p: Gantry 0.27.0 starts the services without --app-root when it connects to a host whose services are stopped. Start the services from the terminal with the flag first; Gantry then uses the running services.
Gantry can do this move for you: see below.
To free space without losing an image, save it to the external disk and delete it. Load it again when you need it:

ol: Stop the containers that use the disk: container stop <name>.
If the app root is on the disk, stop the services: container system stop.
Eject the disk in Finder, then unplug it.

blocks.p: If the disk goes away while containers run from it, they fail, and writes in progress can be lost. After you connect the disk again, start the services with --app-root, then start the containers.
Gantry runs bind mounts from any disk today: in New Container, add a volume, choose a folder on the external disk and a path in the container.

On an apple/container host, the Storage pane in the System section shows where the data root is, on which disk, and how much space images, containers, snapshots, volumes and kernels use. Move to Another Disk… stops the services, copies the data, checks it, switches the root and starts the services again; it deletes the old copy only after a separate confirmation. Gantry remembers the root for every later start. New volumes can live in a folder on any disk, and when that disk is not connected, Gantry tells you which disk is missing and does not start the containers that need it.

blocks.alt: Gantry Storage pane with the data root on an external disk
blocks.caption: Storage. The data root, its disk and the space in use.

blocks.p: Docker Desktop moves its disk image in Settings ▸ Resources ▸ Advanced ▸ Disk image location. OrbStack added a data location setting in version 0.13.0. See the comparison.

faq.q: Can I store Apple container images on an external drive?
faq.a: Yes. Start the services with container system start --app-root /Volumes/Disk/container. All images, containers, snapshots and volumes then live in that folder.

faq.q: Which file system should the external drive use?
faq.a: APFS. Volumes are sparse disk images and containers need Unix permissions, which exFAT, FAT and NTFS do not have.

faq.q: How do I copy the container data without filling the disk?
faq.a: Use cp -Rp, which kept the sparse volume images small in our test. ditto copied each sparse image at its full size.

faq.q: What happens if I unplug the drive while containers run?
faq.a: The containers that use the disk fail, and data that was not yet written can be lost. Stop the containers and, if the app root is on the disk, the services before you eject it.

faq.q: Does the container CLI remember the new location?
faq.a: No. Pass --app-root to every container system start. container system status shows the root in use as paths.appRoot.

docker-run-to-container.title: Create a container from a docker run command on Mac (docker run to container run)
docker-run-to-container.desc: Paste a docker run command into Gantry and get a ready container form, or convert docker run to Apple's container run by hand: flags that map, flags that do not, and reusable recipes.
docker-run-to-container.h1: Create a container from a docker run command
docker-run-to-container.lead: Most READMEs give a docker run line. Gantry reads that line and fills the New Container form, for a Docker host or for Apple's container tool. This guide shows how, and how to convert the command by hand.
docker-run-to-container.tldr: In short. In Gantry, open New Container, choose Paste Command…, paste the docker run line and click Fill Form. Gantry lists each flag that it cannot use, with the reason. For the CLI, most flags are the same: replace docker run with container run and remove --restart.

ol: Select a host: a Docker host or an apple/container host.
Click Paste Command… and paste the line. Line ends with \, quotes, a $ prompt and sudo are all fine.
Read the preview: the image, the flags that Gantry cannot use, notes, and warnings for this host.
Click Fill Form, check the values, and create the container.

blocks.p: Gantry reads docker run, docker container run, docker create, podman run and container run. Text after &&, ||, ; or | is ignored, with a note.

blocks.alt: Paste Command sheet with a docker run line and the list of unused flags
blocks.caption: Paste Command. The form values and the flags that Gantry cannot use.

blocks.p: About 80 other Docker flags are known: Gantry skips their values correctly and lists them as not used, so nothing is lost without a note.
Some Docker options do not exist on apple/container. Gantry warns about them and leaves them out of the create request:

ul: restart policies (--restart);
CPU fractions such as --cpus 0.5;
the host, none and container: network modes;
ports without a host port, such as -p 80.

blocks.p: On a Docker host, Gantry warns about the apple/container options: the DNS domain and the kernel options.

sections.h: Convert docker run to container run by hand

blocks.p: For the CLI, most flags stay the same. A Redis example:
becomes:
Create the named volume first with container volume create. Remove --restart and round --cpus to a whole number. --platform works as in Docker.

sections.h: Copy a container as a command

blocks.p: The other way works too. Right-click a container, or use the More menu, and choose Copy as Command: Gantry writes a docker run or container run line. It leaves out the defaults of the image, such as its environment and command, so the line stays short. This works for stopped containers as well.

In the New Container sheet, open Recipes and choose Save as Recipe…. Next time, Fill from Recipe gives the same form on any host. Recipes are in ~/Library/Application Support/Gantry/recipes.json, so you can back them up or share them.

ul: Gantry keeps the path of --env-file but does not read the file, and does not read your shell for -e KEY without a value.
tmpfs mounts and anonymous volumes from --mount are listed as not supported.
Two ports for the same container port (-p 8080:80 -p 8081:80) fill the form, but the form then refuses the duplicate.

blocks.p: Moving a whole setup? Read Move from Docker Desktop to Apple container.

faq.q: How do I convert docker run to container run?
faq.a: Replace docker run with container run. -d, -p, -e, -v, --name, --rm, -it, -w and --entrypoint stay the same. Remove --restart and use whole CPUs. Or paste the line in Gantry and let it fill the form.

faq.q: Can Gantry import a docker run command?
faq.a: Yes. Paste Command… in the New Container sheet reads docker run, docker create, podman run and container run and fills the form.

faq.q: What happens to flags that Gantry does not support?
faq.a: They are listed in the preview with the reason, and they stay in the form in the section From the Pasted Command, so you can check them later.

faq.q: Can I turn a running container back into a docker run command?
faq.a: Yes. Copy as Command in the container menu writes a docker run or container run line for that container.
